aclacinomycin is a potent new anthracyline with an MTD of 150 mg/m 2 when given in five daily doses.
150 mg/M2 given in 5 daily 30 mg/M2 fractions is a MTD for aclacinomycin.

the maximum tolerated dose of the anthracycline antibiotic aclacinomycin given on a five‐day schedule to patients with advanced cancer is 150 mg/m ^{2} ; that the limiting toxicity was myeloppression; that cardiac toxicity is less marked than with other anthracyclines given on a similar schedule; and that no tumor responses were observed.

the development of new anticancer drugs and their clinical evaluation.
the development of a method of determining the optimal drug dosage for a particular patient.
the study of the chemical, physical, and biological properties of anthracyclines and anthracyclinones.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
aclacinomycin is an anthracycline that is active and well tolerated, and is a candidate for further clinical investigation.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
aclacinomycin has a therapeutic index comparable to doxorubicin.
the new anthrocalyne, aclacinomycin, is a promising drug with a favorable toxicity profile, which may be more active than doxorubicin and less cardiotoxic than doxorubicins and daunorubicins.

the anthracyclines doxorubicin (Adriamycin), daunorubicin, and idarubicin are more active than mitoxantrone, but less active than aclacinomycin, when administered on a five‐day schedule, with the exception that mitoxantrome is more active against breast cancer.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the schedule of drug administration can be a critical variable in the design of Phase I clinical trials.
the five‐day schedule may have less myelosuppressive toxicity and more antitumor activity than single‐dose administration.
the MTD of aclacinomycins can be increased significantly by giving them as a five daily dose regimen rather than as a single dose.
